title: Gavaskar Slams Domestic Format: 'How Does a Team Learn to Take 20 Wickets?'
excerpt: In his Mid-Day column, the batting legend cited the Duleep Trophy final — where East Zone batted on and shook hands instead of pushing for an outright win — to explain India's Test struggles.
body:
• Sunil Gavaskar used the Duleep Trophy 2026 final as a case study in his Mid-Day column, arguing that domestic cricket's culture of settling for first-innings leads is "one of the main reasons India struggle to take 20 wickets on good pitches."
  • East Zone beat South Zone on a 372-run first-innings lead (708 vs 336) after batted-on second innings of 388/7, with both captains shaking hands to end the match early on Day 5 instead of playing for an outright win.
  • Gavaskar linked the mentality directly to the senior team, citing India's failure to bowl Sri Lanka out on the final day of the second Test in Colombo, when the hosts survived from 229/6 to earn a draw.

Sunil Gavaskar has pointed to the Duleep Trophy 2026 final as Exhibit A for why India struggles to take 20 wickets in Test matches. In his column for Mid-Day, the batting legend criticized East Zone's approach in the final against South Zone at the MA Chidambaram Stadium — and the wider domestic culture it represents — of settling for a first-innings lead instead of chasing an outright win.

The final that triggered it

East Zone dominated the final. They piled up 708 in their first innings — captain Ishan Kishan smashing 270 — bowled South Zone out for 336, and secured a 372-run lead. What happened next drew Gavaskar's ire: East Zone batted on for 100 overs in their second innings, reaching 388/7, before both captains — Kishan and South Zone's Tilak Varma — shook hands to end the match early on Day 5. East Zone took the trophy, their first Duleep title in 13 years since 2012-13, solely on the first-innings advantage.

"The disappointing part was that East Zone did not go for an outright win and instead prolonged their second innings unnecessarily. That both skippers agreed to end the game earlier than scheduled also doesn't sit well. If the game was to be stopped early, then why wasn't it stopped at lunch time itself, when it was clear that in the two sessions remaining, South Zone was never going to chase down a score more than 650 runs."

— Sunil Gavaskar, Mid-Day column

Gavaskar's diagnosis

The core of Gavaskar's argument: when domestic results routinely get decided on first-innings leads, bowlers never learn the skill of bowling a team out twice — the defining skill of Test cricket.

"This business of the first innings lead being enough, is one of the main reasons India struggle to take 20 wickets on good pitches. How does a team learn to take 20 wickets if they don't bowl in two innings in a domestic game?"

— Sunil Gavaskar, Mid-Day column

He drew a direct line to the recent past, pointing to the second Test in Sri Lanka, where India "huffed and puffed" on the last day and could not take the last four wickets for victory. Sri Lanka, starting Day 5 at 229/6, batted more than 81 overs and lost just three wickets to finish 429/9 and earn a draw.

Diaspora angle

Gavaskar's critique lands with particular force for diaspora fans who watch India tour and wonder why a team capable of world-class batting spells still struggles to finish sides on flat subcontinent pitches. The Duleep Trophy final was decided by who batted longer, not who bowled better — and Gavaskar's point is that until domestic cricket rewards the second trait, the Test side will keep repeating its Sri Lanka problem.

What's next

East Zone's title ends a 13-year wait, and Kishan's 270 was the standout individual performance. But Gavaskar's larger question — whether the BCCI should restructure domestic first-class incentives to reward outright wins — is one the board has wrestled with for years without resolving. The next marker will be how India's attack performs when it next needs to bowl a side out twice on a good pitch, and whether the lessons of Colombo stick.
